## Why disclose?

If you use an AI system (such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Copilot) at any
stage of your academic work, you are expected to **document what you did and
disclose it transparently**. Doing so is not an admission that you cut corners —
it is part of good scientific practice. It lets readers judge how your results
came about, protects you against accusations of academic misconduct, and forces
you to reflect critically on where the AI actually helped and where it did not.

The core principle is simple:

> While AI tools may assist your work, **you remain fully responsible** for every
> claim, analysis, and conclusion you submit.

A disclosure should tell a reader what the AI did and how you made sure the
result is sound. It does not need to retrace your work with the tool. This page
gives you (1) a short **template** to include in your work, (2) a **worked
example**, and (3) a note on how to **cite** AI in your reference list. Always
check the concrete requirements of your specific course or examination
regulations — this template is a sensible default, not a rule that overrides
them. If in doubt, clarify this topic with your instructor _as early as
possible_.

## The disclosure template (fill this in)

Copy the table into an appendix or to the end of your work and add the
statement of responsibility below it. If you did not use any AI tool, write
"No AI tools were used." and you are done.

| Element | What to include | Your entry |
|---|---|---|
| **Tool** | Name of the system, model or version (as far as it is shown to you), how you accessed it (browser, app, API, IDE plugin), and your subscription plan (free or which paid plan). | |
| **Used for** | What the AI did, and in which parts of your work (e.g. finding literature, feedback on the structure of a section, debugging code, translating a passage). | |
| **What I checked** | How you checked the output, and against what. | |
| **What I changed** | What you corrected or discarded as a result — or that nothing needed changing. | |
| **My own** | The parts of the work done without AI. | |
| **Personal or confidential data** | *Only if you entered any:* what it was and why this was permitted. | |

### Statement of responsibility

Close your disclosure with this statement, adapted if necessary:

> I checked all AI output that I used and take full responsibility for the
> content of this work.

## What you do not need to report

- **Prompts, chat logs, or the number of attempts** — you do not hand these in.
- **Exact dates of access.**
- **Spelling and grammar checks** that only correct errors, and the routine
  functions of a reference manager. Once a tool rewrites sentences, reorganises
  a text, or translates it, this counts as use and belongs in the table.
- **General weaknesses of AI tools.** Mention a problem only if it affected
  your work, under *What I checked* or *What I changed*.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Keep your chats until your work is graded
Although you do not submit them, your chats let you answer questions about how
a passage or result came about. Journals and other institutions may ask for
more than this template does, so check their rules when you publish.
:::

## Worked example

The following shows the template filled in for a fictional Management-Studies
term paper.

| Element | Example entry |
|---|---|
| **Tool** | Claude (Sonnet 5), Anthropic; in the browser; Pro plan. |
| **Used for** | Synonyms for my concept table · feedback on the structure of section 2 · debugging the R code for the descriptive statistics. |
| **What I checked** | Each suggested term in the database · the code by rerunning it and calculating one variable by hand. |
| **What I changed** | Dropped four terms not used in the literature · rewrote section 2 myself, adopting only the feedback I agreed with. |
| **My own** | Research question, screening of the literature, analysis, all conclusions. |

> I checked all AI output that I used and take full responsibility for the
> content of this work.

## Citing AI in your reference list

Disclosure (the table above) and citation (an entry in your bibliography) are
**complementary**, not interchangeable. Most style guides now treat generative
AI as a retrievable source. In **APA 7**, for example, the author is the company
that made the model, and the format is roughly:

> Anthropic. (2026). *Claude* (Sonnet model) [Large language model]. https://claude.ai

Check the current guidance for the citation style your course requires (APA, MLA,
Chicago, or the journal style used in this module), as recommendations for AI
sources are still evolving. Personally, I find acknowledging and documenting the
use of AI far more useful and important than citing an AI model.
